title: CausaFlow — An Urban Flood Forensic Lab
pitch: An agent-ready flood lab where people ask “what if?” and WebMCP agents safely run, inspect, replay, and compare flood scenarios with every assumption visible.
about_excerpt: An agent-ready flood lab where people ask “what if?” and WebMCP agents safely run, inspect, replay, and compare flood scenarios with every assumption visible. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Flood simulations can be difficult to use and even harder to explain. A person may need to choose a location, configure a scenario, review assumptions, start a long-running calculation, inspect several results, replay the flood, and compare it with another run. An AI agent looking only at buttons and pixels could easily choose the wrong setup or mistake the colour of an animation for a real result. I built CausaFlow to solve both problems. It is an urban flood investigation lab where a person asks the question and a WebMCP agent safely handles the multi-step work inside the application. What CausaFlow does CausaFlow lets people explore flood situations in two study areas: Texas Medical Center and Brays Bayou in Houston Velachery and its surrounding area in Chennai In Houston, CausaFlow can test heavy rain, a river carrying more water than its assumed capacity, or blocked drains along a hospital access road. In Velachery, it can keep rain off the city itself while applying severe rain around its boundary, then show which monitored neighbourhoods are affected first. Each completed run provides more than an animation. It reports water depth, speed, affected area, arrival times, water accounting, assumptions, limitations, and result identities that can be checked later. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Flood investigation is not a single-button task. It is a chain of connected decisions and actions. Without WebMCP, an agent would have to guess its way through a complex 3D interface. It could select the wrong scenario, run an outdated setup, lose track of which result is displayed, or describe what the animation appears to show instead of reading the actual numbers. WebMCP gives the agent direct access to clearly defined actions and exact application state. The agent knows which study area is active, which scenario is staged, whether the user has approved it, which calculation is running, which result is displayed, and what the result actually says. This makes CausaFlow faster and easier to use while keeping the person in control. What people and agents can do together The person provides the goal, judgment, and approval. The agent handles the repeated application work. For example, a person can ask: Block every represented drain along the hospital access road, show when the route becomes unsafe, then reopen the fewest drains needed and run the same storm again. The WebMCP agent can then: Open the correct Houston study area. Place the represented drains along the access road. Stage the blocked scenario. Show the assumptions on screen. Wait for the person’s explicit approval. Start and monitor the flood calculation. Read the completed numerical result. Save it as the comparison case. Run the tested intervention under the same storm. Compare both results and move the camera to the important location. Completing that entire sequence manually would require navigating several controls and carefully tracking two separate results. With WebMCP, the person can remain focused on the investigation while the agent handles the mechanics. Every important action remains visible in the interface, and the normal controls remain available as a fallback. How I implemented WebMCP I register the application’s tools directly through document.modelContext.registerTool . The tools are divided into two groups: Flood tools for inspecting capabilities, staging scenarios, requesting approval, starting calculations, monitoring progress, reading results, controlling playback, sampling locations, and comparing runs. Workspace tools for changing study areas, reading the visible scene, moving the camera, and focusing on important results. Each tool has a clear description and a strict input format. Tools that only read information are marked separately from tools that change the application. CausaFlow also protects the workflow in several ways: A calculation cannot begin until the exact staged scenario has been approved. Every scenario change creates a new revision, preventing an agent from approving an older setup by mistake. The user’s request to run a scenario is recorded as explicit authorization. Long-running calculations return progress instead of leaving the agent guessing. Completed results have stable identities and cannot be silently changed during replay or comparison. The agent reads numerical results from the application instead of estimating values from the animation. WebMCP is the access and coordination layer. It does not create the flood results. The calculations come from the flood-simulation software used by CausaFlow. Key demonstration: Hospital Lifeline Hospital Lifeline represents eight drains along a 771-metre hospital access road. With every represented drain blocked, the access checkpoint crosses its 15-centimetre test limit after 270 seconds and reaches a maximum depth of approximately 32.8 centimetres. I tested the zero-drain case and every individual-drain alternative. Reopening D7 was the only single-drain option that kept the checkpoint below the limit. Its maximum depth fell to approximately 12.7 centimetres, and D7 removed approximately 311.6 cubic metres of water. The WebMCP agent can run the blocked case, run the D7 case under the same storm, compare them, and take the user directly to the checkpoint. How I built it I built the interface with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Three.js, and deck.gl. The flood calculations run through ANUGA using Python. I also use EPA SWMM for separate drainage checks. Houston uses frozen USGS elevation data. Velachery uses frozen Copernicus elevation data with OpenStreetMap context. I packaged the application with Docker and deployed it through Coolify. Challenges I faced The first challenge was keeping the agent helpful without giving it too much control. I solved this by exposing small, clearly limited tools instead of one unrestricted command. The second challenge was preventing stale or unapproved scenarios from running. I added revision checks and explicit approval before every calculation. The third challenge was making sure the agent reported real results rather than guessing from the animation. The result tools return exact values, assumptions, warnings, and limitations. I also had to make the flood calculations, terrain files, interface, WebMCP tools, and production deployment work together inside one Docker container. Accomplishments I’m proud of Five complete flood demonstration flows A multi-step WebMCP workflow that works without clicking simulation controls A safe approval boundary before calculations begin Direct result inspection instead of visual guessing Result replay, camera control, and comparison through WebMCP 74 unit and regression tests 23 flood-calculation checks 11 production browser tests A public Docker deployment with no login
video_transcript_excerpt: Tell me how what does this application offer? What can I do with it? How many Web MCP endpoints are available? >> One sec. I'll check. It's a voice controllable flood simulation lab for real terrain in Houston's Medical Center and Velachery, Chennai. And it has 21 Web MCP endpoints. You can inspect terrain and solver state. Choose a place, set up heavy rain or overflow scenarios, run and monitor simulations, replay results, sample depth and speed at points, focus on impacted spots, and compare runs. >> Okay. Take me to Houston and show me the whole Medical Center area. Let's start simple. Let's set up the standard heavy rain simulation and run it. >> Sure. I'll set that up. The standard Houston Medical Center run finished and the result is displayed across the full area. That was the 5-minute rain pulse peaking at 120 mm per hour. >> Okay. Play the flood from beginning. When it finishes, tell me how deep the water became, how fast it moved, how much ground was covered, and when the underpass first became a problem. >> Okay. I'll start the replay and watch for those points. The replay finished. Peak depth was about 9.3 cm. Peak speed 0.34 m per second. And roughly 1.89 square kilometers got wet. The Brays Bayou underpass first crossed its problem threshold at 4 and 1/2 minutes peaking near 7.2 cm for about 30 seconds. These are planning preview numbers. >> Okay. Uh now remove the rain completely. Send a heavy surge down Brays Bayou, more water than it can hold. Show me the water moving down the river and spilling out. Tell me which important places affected first and take me there when it happens. >> Got it. I'll check that. There's a matching preset for that Brays Bayou overflow with no rain. >> Mhm. >> The Bayou overflow run is in progress. >> Okay, which part was most affected? >> Let me pull that up. The no rain overflow run completed and is playing. I've moved you to the first affected spot at its arrival time. The most affected monitored place was the Houston Methodist Child Care Center access point. Water arrived at 5 minutes and peaked around 1.64 m. The Brays Bayou Greenway access was second, near 86 cm. This is a modeled screen result, not an observed emergency finding. Houston is still selected. I staged eight clear simulated drains along the medical center access road at 80 m intervals, 560 m total. I haven't run a new simulation yet and those drain locations are just screening assumptions. >> Okay, block every simulated drain along this road and run the same heavy rain. Show me when the hospital access road becomes unsafe. Then reopen the first two drains nearer to keep the road below its limit and rerun the exact same storm. >> Let me check all of that carefully. The first run is active now with all eight drains closed and the hospital heavy rain locked in at 250. >> Okay, I see the simulation. >> For context, with all drains blocked, the medical center access road crossed its limit at 4 and 1/2 minutes, peaked near 32.8 cm, and stayed over for the final 5 and 1/2 minutes. I've got the view at that arrival moment. Switching to >> Now, take me to Velachery. Start wide so I can see the area around it, then bring me closer to the city. >> All right, let me pull that up. You're now in Velachery. I opened the wide surrounding view first, then moved in closer over the city. The location and camera are set, though some terrain detail is still loading. >> Okay, fine. Uh no. Select the preset that keeps the rain off Villatery itself, but make it rain severely around its boundary. Run the flood and show me which monitored parts of Villatery crossed their warning levels first. Play the whole animation, then take me to the hardest hit monitored place. >> There is a surrounding rain preset for that. The perimeter rain simulation is running now. >> Got it. Okay, what are the results? >> Let me pull those up. Two of six monitored areas crossed their warning level. Nerunagar's north edge crossed first, followed later by Baljinaga

live_observation.first_impression: A cinematic landing page leads with 'Ask the city why it floods' and an OPEN LAB call to action. The flood-forensics purpose is clear but the initial screen contains little operational detail.
live_observation.after_state: Scenario setup opened for the Texas Medical Center/Brays Bayou model, with area, forcing, and run-mode controls plus assumption/runtime review actions. No simulation run was started.
live_observation.notes: The central workflow is visibly structured around configuring a flood scenario before running it.
